title: How does `ServiceLoader` (the Java SPI mechanism) discover implementations (`META-INF/services` files, lazy loading via the context classloader)?
shortTitle: How does ServiceLoader (the Java SPI mechanism) discover implementations?

s1_definition.profdef: `ServiceLoader` is Java's built-in Service Provider Interface mechanism for discovering and loading implementations of an interface at run time without the consumer naming the implementation classes directly. You define a service interface, and provider jars advertise their implementations either with a classpath text file at `META-INF/services/fully.qualified.InterfaceName` listing implementation class names, or, in a modular application, with a `provides ... with` directive in `module-info.java`. The consumer calls `ServiceLoader.load(Interface.class)` and iterates the discovered providers. Loading is lazy, implementations are instantiated only as you iterate, and on the classpath discovery uses a class loader, commonly the thread's context class loader, to find the provider files.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants to accept fee calculators from different vendors without the core system ever hard-coding a vendor's name. The bank publishes a standard job description, the service interface, saying "a fee calculator must compute a fee for an account." Any vendor who wants to be hired simply drops a signed card into a well-known mailbox, the META-INF services file, that says "my class fulfills that job description." When the bank needs fee calculators, it opens the mailbox, reads every card, and hires each listed vendor, creating them only as it actually needs them. The core system never knew any vendor by name; it just trusted the mailbox and the job description.
s1_definition.oneliner: ServiceLoader discovers implementations of an interface by reading provider declarations, META-INF/services files on the classpath or provides directives in modules, and lazily instantiates them, decoupling consumers from concrete providers.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ServiceLoader` is Java's built-in Service Provider Interface mechanism for discovering and loading implementations of an interface at run time without the consumer naming the implementation classes directly. You define a service interface, and provider jars advertise their implementations either with a classpath text file at `META-INF/services/fully.qualified.InterfaceName` listing implementation class names, or, in a modular application, with a `provides ... with` directive in `module-info.java`. The consumer calls `ServiceLoader.load(Interface.class)` and iterates the discovered providers. Loading is lazy, implementations are instantiated only as you iterate, and on the classpath discovery uses a class loader, commonly the thread's context class loader, to find the provider files.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants to accept fee calculators from different vendors without the core system ever hard-coding a vendor's name. The bank publishes a standard job description, the service interface, saying "a fee calculator must compute a fee for an account." Any vendor who wants to be hired simply drops a signed card into a well-known mailbox, the META-INF services file, that says "my class fulfills that job description." When the bank needs fee calculators, it opens the mailbox, reads every card, and hires each listed vendor, creating them only as it actually needs them. The core system never knew any vendor by name; it just trusted the mailbox and the job description.

**One line to remember:** ServiceLoader discovers implementations of an interface by reading provider declarations, META-INF/services files on the classpath or provides directives in modules, and lazily instantiates them, decoupling consumers from concrete providers.

sections.s2_technical:
The Service Provider Interface pattern separates three roles. The service is an interface or abstract class that defines a capability. The service provider is a concrete implementation of that interface, usually shipped in its own jar or module. The service consumer is the code that needs the capability but should not depend on any specific provider. `ServiceLoader` is the runtime machinery that connects consumers to providers without a compile-time dependency, which is how the JDK itself loads JDBC drivers, charset providers, logging backends, and many other pluggable pieces.

On the classpath, a provider advertises itself with a plain text file. If the service interface is `com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator`, the provider jar contains a file named `META-INF/services/com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator`, and each line of that file is the fully-qualified name of an implementation class, for example `com.vendor.gst.GstFeeCalculator`. There can be several lines for several implementations, and blank lines and comments starting with a hash are ignored. When multiple provider jars are on the classpath, all of their files for that interface are found, so you can have many providers from many jars.

The consumer calls `ServiceLoader.load(FeeCalculator.class)`. This returns a `ServiceLoader` that is lazy and iterable. The crucial point is laziness: the loader does not read all the files and instantiate everything up front. Instead, as you iterate, it locates the next provider declaration, loads that class, and instantiates it, one at a time. This matters because you might stop after finding a suitable provider, and because instantiating a provider can be expensive or can fail, and lazy iteration lets you handle failures per provider. In modern Java, `ServiceLoader.stream()` goes further by giving you `Provider` handles that let you inspect the provider type before deciding to instantiate it, so you can filter without constructing.

Discovery needs a class loader to find the files and classes, and by default `ServiceLoader.load(Service.class)` uses the current thread's context class loader. The context class loader exists precisely for this situation: a framework class, loaded by a parent loader, needs to load provider classes that live in a child loader, such as the application's loader, which the strict parent-delegation model would not normally reach. The thread context class loader is a back-channel that frameworks set so that service discovery sees application-level providers. You can also pass an explicit class loader with the two-argument `ServiceLoader.load(Service.class, classLoader)` when you need precise control, which is common in application servers and plugin containers where each deployment has its own loader.

Providers loaded via the classpath file mechanism must, by default, have a public no-argument constructor, because `ServiceLoader` instantiates them reflectively with no arguments. If a provider needs construction logic, the modern approach is a static provider method named `provider` that returns an instance, which the loader will use instead of the constructor.

In the module system the mechanism is declarative rather than text-file based. The provider module writes `provides com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator with com.vendor.gst.GstFeeCalculator;` in its `module-info.java`, and the consumer module writes `uses com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator;`. The compiler and the module system verify these declarations, so a missing or misspelled provider is caught earlier than with a plain text file, and the module graph records the service relationships. `ServiceLoader.load` then resolves providers from the module layer. A modular application can also keep backward compatibility by still honoring `META-INF/services` files for automatic modules.

A few senior nuances. Service loading is unordered; you should not rely on the order providers appear, and if you need priority you add your own ranking, often via an annotation or a method on the interface, and sort the discovered providers yourself. Iterating a `ServiceLoader` can throw `ServiceConfigurationError` if a declared provider is missing, is not actually a subtype, or fails to instantiate, so robust consumers iterate defensively and skip bad providers. And because discovery is tied to a class loader, the same application run under different loaders can see different providers, which is intended for isolation but can surprise you. The payoff of all this is genuine extensibility: you add a capability to a running system by dropping a new jar or module on the path, with zero changes to the consumer code.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's billing engine must support several fee calculators, a goods-and-services-tax calculator, a flat-fee calculator, and vendor-specific ones, and new calculators must be addable without editing or recompiling the billing engine. This is exactly the Service Provider Interface case: define a `FeeCalculator` interface and discover implementations with `ServiceLoader`, so the engine never names a concrete calculator.

Problem 2 — A vendor ships a new calculator jar months later. We want the engine to pick it up just by placing the jar on the classpath. This is the META-INF services case: the vendor's jar declares its implementation in a provider file, and `ServiceLoader` finds it automatically.

Problem 3 — The engine should not instantiate calculators it does not need, and a broken provider should not crash the whole engine. This is the lazy-loading and defensive-iteration case: providers are instantiated only as iterated, and we skip any that fail.

The mini-project defines the `FeeCalculator` service, provides two implementations declared in a `META-INF/services` file, and a billing engine that loads all calculators via `ServiceLoader`, applies each to Rajesh and Priya, and sums the fees, all without naming any implementation.

The code contains: the `FeeCalculator` interface; two provider classes; the provider declaration file; and a billing engine that uses `ServiceLoader`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and ensure the META-INF/services file is on the classpath
javac -d out $(find src/main/java -name "*.java")
cp -r src/main/resources/META-INF out/META-INF
java -cp out com.bank.billing.BillingEngine

# Modular equivalent (module-info.java):
#   provider module:  provides com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator with com.bank.spi.impl.GstFeeCalculator;
#   consumer module:  uses com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator;
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a billing run for Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250000), with fee calculators discovered at run time.

Step 1: `ServiceLoader.load(FeeCalculator.class)` creates a lazy loader. It will use the thread's context class loader to find provider declarations. Nothing is read or instantiated yet.

Step 2: The engine calls `iterator()` and starts iterating. On the first `next`, the loader reads the `META-INF/services/com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator` file, finds the first line, `GstFeeCalculator`, loads that class, and instantiates it with its no-arg constructor.

Step 3: The engine applies the GST calculator. For Rajesh, 0.1 percent of Rs.1000000 is Rs.1000.00, plus 18 percent GST equals Rs.1180.00. For Priya, 0.1 percent of Rs.250000 is Rs.250.00, plus GST equals Rs.295.00.

Step 4: The next `next` lazily loads and instantiates `FlatFeeCalculator`. It returns a flat Rs.50.00 for each of Rajesh and Priya.

Step 5: Had a declared provider been missing or broken, `next` would throw `ServiceConfigurationError`, and the engine catches it and skips that provider, so one bad vendor jar cannot crash billing.

Step 6: The engine sums per customer. Rajesh total is Rs.1180.00 plus Rs.50.00 equals Rs.1230.00; Priya total is Rs.295.00 plus Rs.50.00 equals Rs.345.00. The engine never named a single implementation; dropping a new vendor jar with its own provider file would add a calculator automatically.

```
Oct 26, 2026 3:48:00 PM com.bank.billing.BillingEngine main
INFO: Provider GST-18% → Rajesh Rs.1180.00, Priya Rs.295.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:48:00 PM com.bank.billing.BillingEngine main
INFO: Provider FLAT-50 → Rajesh Rs.50.00, Priya Rs.50.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:48:00 PM com.bank.billing.BillingEngine main
INFO: Total fees — Rajesh: Rs.1230.00, Priya: Rs.345.00
```

```
    │   line1: GstFeeCalculator   ─next()─→ load + new() ─┐
    │   line2: FlatFeeCalculator  ─next()─→ load + new() ─┤ (instantiated only when iterated)

    │ GST  : Rajesh 1,000,000×0.001×1.18 = Rs.1180.00 ; Priya Rs.295.00

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ServiceLoader is Java's built-in Service Provider Interface mechanism for discovering and loading implementations of an interface at run time without the consumer ever naming the concrete classes. The pattern has three roles: the service, which is the interface defining a capability; the provider, which is a concrete implementation shipped in its own jar or module; and the consumer, which needs the capability but should not depend on any specific provider. ServiceLoader is the runtime machinery that connects them, and it is how the JDK itself loads JDBC drivers, charset providers, and logging backends.

Discovery works in one of two ways. On the classpath, a provider jar contains a plain text file at META-INF slash services slash the fully-qualified interface name, and each line is the fully-qualified name of an implementation class. All such files across all jars are found, so you can have many providers. In the module system it is declarative instead: the provider module writes provides the interface with the implementation in its module-info, and the consumer writes uses the interface, which the compiler and module system verify so mistakes are caught earlier. The consumer calls ServiceLoader dot load with the interface class and iterates the result. Two properties are important. First, loading is lazy: providers are instantiated only as you iterate, which skips unused providers and lets you handle a per-provider failure without crashing. Second, discovery needs a class loader to find the declarations, and by default it uses the thread's context class loader, which is the back-channel frameworks use so that discovery can reach application-level providers that strict parent-delegation would not normally see; you can also pass an explicit loader for precise control in app servers and plugin containers.

In my work at National Bank of India I used this for a billing engine that had to support several fee calculators and allow new ones without editing the engine. I defined a FeeCalculator interface, shipped GST and flat-fee providers declared in a META-INF services file, and the engine loaded them all with ServiceLoader, applied each to Rajesh and Priya, and summed the fees, never naming a single implementation. Months later a vendor could add a calculator just by dropping a jar with its own provider file on the path, discovered automatically. The senior points I always add are that service loading is unordered, so if I need priority I add my own ranking and sort, that iterating can throw a ServiceConfigurationError for a missing or broken provider so robust consumers skip bad ones defensively, and that providers loaded from the classpath file need a public no-argument constructor or a static provider method. The payoff is genuine extensibility: I add a capability to a running system by dropping in a jar or module, with zero changes to the consumer.
